Good web design in Oklahoma City starts with a map of districts, not a map of the city. A customer here rarely searches for "shops in OKC." They look for dinner in the Asian District, vintage clothes on the Plaza, a gallery walk in the Paseo or a saddle in Stockyards City. Each of those places has its own crowd, its own events and its own reputation, and a small business inside one competes first with its neighbors on the same few blocks. A website that just says "proudly serving Oklahoma City" misses the way people here actually shop.

Dominion Web Design Pro is Maurice Johnson, one person building sites from Big Sandy in East Texas. Every page is written by hand, you see a free demo before you pay, and the price is printed: $497, $997 or $1,997, one time.

A penny tax that rebuilt downtown

Much of today's district map traces back to a vote in December 1993. Oklahoma City residents approved MAPS, the Metropolitan Area Projects, a temporary one-cent sales tax that paid cash for big public projects instead of borrowing. The first round built the Bricktown ballpark, the Bricktown Canal, a downtown arena and work on the convention center, among other projects.

Voters kept coming back. MAPS for Kids followed in 2001 for school buildings, MAPS 3 in 2009 brought Scissortail Park and new trails, and MAPS 4 passed on December 10, 2019, with close to a billion dollars aimed at parks, transit, mental health, homelessness and more. Local writers credit the program with drawing people back downtown, and once people came back, the older commercial strips around the core had customers again.

Which OKC district is yours, and what its customers look for

Each district draws a different visitor. Here is what that means for the first page of your site.

DistrictWhere and what it is known forWhat your site should make obvious
Automobile AlleyBroadway just north of downtown, once lined with car dealerships, now shops, restaurants and nightlife under the old neon signsEvening hours, parking along Broadway and what makes your place worth the stop
Plaza DistrictNW 16th Street between Classen and Pennsylvania, 45 or more businesses, vintage shops, the restored Plaza Theatre and the LIVE on the Plaza art walk each second FridayWhether you stay open for the art walk and what is new on the racks or the menu
Paseo Arts DistrictSpanish revival buildings with more than 20 galleries, more than 80 working artists and a First Friday gallery walkStudio hours, how to buy or commission work, and a calendar that is actually current
Asian DistrictClassen Boulevard, roughly NW 23rd to NW 30th, shaped by Vietnamese families who arrived in the 1970s, now Vietnamese, Chinese, Thai and other restaurants and marketsThe menu as real text, dish names spelled the way people search them, hours and a map
Stockyards CityBeside the Oklahoma National Stockyards, open since 1910, with cattle auctions Mondays and Tuesdays, western wear stores and steakhousesAuction day hours, what you carry and whether you ship, for buyers who drove in from out of town
Bricktown and Film RowThe MAPS ballpark and canal on the east side of downtown; Film Row, which one guide counts as part of the downtown Arts District, with a growing restaurant and nightlife sceneGame night and event night plans, walking directions and reservations

Web design in Oklahoma City that keeps up with district events

District life runs on a calendar. The Plaza District has its monthly art walk and an annual festival that draws close to 20,000 people. The Paseo has First Friday. Stockyards City has auction days twice a week. Those are the moments when strangers walk past your door, pull out a phone and decide where to go next. If your hours, your specials or your "open late tonight" note live only on a social media post from three weeks ago, many of them will never find it.

Google says local results depend mainly on relevance, distance and prominence. For a district business, relevance and distance both lean on the district name: someone standing on NW 16th searching "vintage store near me" is close to you, and your site should confirm in plain words that you are right there. That means the district and cross streets in your page title and opening line, an events or hours page you can keep current, and the same name, address and phone on your site and your Google Business Profile. Nobody honest can promise you a ranking, and we will not. We can make sure your site says clearly where you are and when you are open.

Beyond the districts: the base, the suburbs and the offices that serve them

Not every Oklahoma City business sells to weekend crowds. Tinker Air Force Base, on the southeast side of the metro, is the largest single-site employer in Oklahoma, with more than 26,000 military and civilian workers according to the base's own fact sheet. Those workers buy houses, fix cars, see dentists, hire roofers and need childcare. The Oklahoma City metro was home to about 1.51 million people in the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate.

For a dentist near Midwest City, a home inspector in Moore or a plumber who covers Del City and Choctaw, the district map matters less than the list of towns. Those owners need a service area page that names the places they really work, and, where the work justifies it, a separate page for each town written about that town. That is exactly what the city pages in the Pro and Agency packages are for.

When customers search the whole state

Some searches here are not about the city at all. People type "website design Oklahoma," "Oklahoma website design" and "web design in Oklahoma" when they are a contractor in Lawton, a ranch supply store in Enid or a clinic in Ardmore looking for help without a big agency bill. Oklahoma is a small business state: the SBA Office of Advocacy's 2025 profile counted about 395,520 small businesses, 99.4 percent of all businesses in the state, employing 50.8 percent of its workers. We work the same way for any of them. The site is written about your town, not a generic "Oklahoma" page, and everything happens by phone and email.

Free help for Oklahoma City owners

  • Oklahoma Small Business Development Center. A statewide network headquartered at Southeastern Oklahoma State University. Rose State College hosts a full-service office in Midwest City that serves start-ups and existing businesses across the Oklahoma City metro.
  • SCORE Oklahoma City. Free, confidential mentoring from experienced business people, with an office at 318 NW 13th Street and workshops through the year.
  • Greater Oklahoma City Chamber. Its small business assistance page points owners to local and state programs, including the SBDC partnership.
  • The Alliance for Economic Development of Oklahoma City. A nonprofit that carries out economic development work under contracts with the city and related public bodies, a useful contact if you are expanding or relocating.

Common questions

How much does website design in Oklahoma City cost?

Quotes in the metro run from a few hundred dollars for a template to thousands for an agency build, and many firms only price after a meeting. Our prices are printed: Starter is $497 for a five-page site, Pro is $997 for ten pages plus ten city pages, and Agency is $1,997 for keyword research and a page for each town and service worth having. All are one time. Hosting, maintenance and updates are $49 a month, or included while you keep the AI agent.

Do I need an OKC web design company with an office in town?

Only if meeting in person matters more to you than seeing the work first. We have no Oklahoma City office. Maurice Johnson builds every site himself from East Texas, and you see a free demo of your own site before paying anything. If you would rather sit across a desk from your designer, a local firm is the better fit, and that is a fair choice.

Do you do website design for Oklahoma businesses outside the city?

Yes. Edmond, Norman, Moore, Midwest City, Tulsa or a small town two hours out all work the same way, because everything happens by phone, email and shared links. If you serve several towns, the Pro package includes ten city pages, each one researched and written about that place.

Should my website mention my district, like the Plaza District or Paseo?

If you are in one, yes, plainly and early. People search for the district by name when they plan an evening or a shopping trip, and district events like a monthly art walk send visitors looking for who is open late. Put the district name in your page title, your first paragraph and your Google Business Profile, along with cross streets and parking.

Can you build an online store for my OKC shop?

Not inside these packages. They are built to bring in calls, visits and form leads, not to run a full online store with inventory and checkout. If selling online is the main goal, say so when you ask for the demo and we will tell you honestly whether we are the right fit.

See your website before you pay for it

Give us your business name and what you do, and a demo site gets built for you to look at on your own phone. If you like it, pick a package. If you do not, you have spent nothing but the minute it took to look.
